children.author: betterunix2
children.text:
> Scott is likely seeing his career prospects disappear in front of his eyes

Why would he be seeing that?

The combination of a mathematician and lean is powerful, and the combination of a mathematician, lean, and AI is more powerful still. Note that the mathematician is always part of that picture. That is fundamental -- no software system, no matter how big and complicated, can actually solve every math problem (this is a fundamental result in math that started the entire field of computer science). If you read TFA he basically tells you what he is actually worrying about here:

"the Lean formal verification system still has issues, from kernel bugs (which have, in the past, allowed proofs of 0=1) to uncertain soundness of the underlying type theory. In my view, these issues can and should urgently be fixed! Until they are, a sufficiently motivated AI could almost certainly exploit them to prove a false statement!"

He is worried about the proof checking system and the possibility that an AI might exploit bugs in the proof checker, not the disintegration of his entire career because AI can "just figure it all out" or whatever.

Isn't it obvious? Scott Aaronson is a theoretical computer scientist, which is essentially a mathematician. Scott is likely seeing his career prospects disappear in front of his eyes just like so many others.

Too many people only see the perils of something once it affects them.

The optimists think AI will be like the cotton gin where making something cheaper and more accessible actually increased the demand for slaves as the price dropped. I'm more pessimistic. A lot of jobs are going to collapse in demand in the coming years. For awhile those at or near the top will survive and possibly make a lot of money but the rising floodwaters come for everybody.

But then you leave the training distribution and you get disturbed by how poor the performance is and how obviously equivalent things don't automatically transfer at all. > Airliners are still subsonic after a 100 years of aviation.

Yeah, but that's a choice made for very good reasons:

- Noise reduction

- Fuel efficiency

- Reduced pollution and lower environment impact

- Reduced cost of materials, equipment, and maintenance

- Passenger affordability

It's not that we can't make supersonic airliners or that the fact we don’t illustrates a lack of progress or performance: it's that it doesn't make economic or environmental sense to.

Gulfstream and Sukhoi even had a partnership to develop a supersonic business jet (which, if you look at the mockups, might be one of the coolest looking planes ever conceived) but they gave up after spending a fairly enormous amount of money already because it was going to cost an absolute fortune to bring to market... and there was no real market for it.

It does not. If after careful analysis people conclude that they cannot tell if it says what it claims to say, then then it can be considered not-a-proof until someone can demonstrate in a convincing manner that it is what it claims to be.

I can say god exists because 5>3. No matter how valid my claim is that five is in-fact greater than three, if I can't convince people of the connection it's a valid proof of something, just not what I say it is.

It might be true that if the Riemann hypothesis is false, leaves cannot fall to the ground. That would mean a falling leaf demonstrates the truth of the hypothesis. Without showing people why it must be the case in a way they understand it falls short of a genuine proof.

That would make proofs subjective, and I think that is true. To many people Pythagoras has not been proved, they just believe (correctly) there is a consensus amongst those who do understand the proofs.

All it means is this one stupid machine in this one instance created a big stupid mess. A mess we can understand, if we try.

The answer is, "I cannot explain that force to you. It is just, as a matter of fact, one of the fundamental forces of nature."

He's taking it as read that the reason he is giving his extended answer is to explain why he cannot answer at all.

What he could have said to a physics student is that: wave-functions of charged particles have a property, "phase". The problem is that point values of phase cannot be observed, and if you formulate the laws of physics with raw "phase" values (like a measure of mass, at 5kg), they dont work. So something must exist to "track" phase, so that every pair of measurements "cancel out" the effect of this property. That something is the EM field. Magentism is a spatial aspect of this field. Eletricity is a space-time aspect of this field. So the magnetic force arises out of a need to "conserve phase", and that phase is how a pushing force is experienced: two particles experiencing a magentic interaction take on different phases (their wavefunctions interfere such that..).

This might "feel" like an explanation to the physics student, because they will be willing to make the assumptions needed, and they will find conservation-style explanations sufficiently satisfying. ie., they can already see a wavefn description will have a free phase term. But a lay person wouldnt feel satisfied because more unknowns have been introduced, and conserving "another unknown" is no advancement in understanding.

That's the gulf which is frustrating feynman. There's nothign to be said to the interviewer other than the force has no explanation in terms of anything he's familiar with. The question is too basic. And feynman is not going to go thru a formulation of QM in terms of wavefns in 5min -- it would be an entire lecture course.

Because he projects a certain kind of frustration that's not warranted in that moment. He's being asked a technical question without any means to give a rigorous answer. I appreciate rigorous thinking, but the interviewer doesn't necessarily want a perfectly rigorous answer, nor does the average person. He's not responding to a need, he's projecting his own perfectionism.

The interviewer most likely would not have interrogated him further about the underlying properties of ice (or engaged in that entire fictitious interaction). Feynman clearly understands that there are several levels to understanding.

So just give an answer that you feel is appropriate, add a disclaimer ("this answer is hand wavy"), and move on. Why is that so hard?

Some people i've shown this to (in admiration for Feynman) have had the same reaction, but I just cannot see it. I'd be interested to know why you think he's unpleasant.

Are you a physicist? I wonder if non-physicists just misread his frustration. The question isnt about some macroscopic physics problem that decomposes clearly into something satisfying. Its a question about one of the most basic constituents of reality. A "why?" question about something so basic has no answer other than "just because". Insofar as anything can be said, it will be so abstract and technical that it wont satisfyingly address the question.

It is a little like a lay person asking a mathematician: why is 0*1 = 0, but 0+1=1 ?

Except, somewhat more extreme than that, because such basic things as 'magnetism' are introduced into all accessible physics formalisms as assumptions.

children.text:
My undergrad is in physics and I was the electrical officer on my first ship. There were plenty of exotic things about that plant that stupified me, but it seemed like no one else was interested in those things. All the other junior officers were busy quizzing each other on the number of cylinders in the diesel engines that drove the generators, what spaces the generators were in, shit that didn't really seem to matter to me.

One afternoon underway I was standing in Central Control and the main propulsion assistant, more senior to me and studying for her engineering boards, started quizzing me about the electrical plant. And I would explain things. And she would ask why. So I would explain and she would ask why. And so on. Until we got to fundamental wave equation for electromagnetism. And she kept asking why. And at one point I realized we were at the bottom. There's nothing really below electromagnetism. It just is. And I said that. "It's one of the 4 fundamental forces. It's just a mathematical description of the way the world seems to work, and it's proven to be correct, entirely, in all cases. There other forces at different energy levels, but in the world that affects you and me, it just is. It, it just is."

And at that point I realized half the engineering department was peeking in from around the consoles. And she starting crying. And I felt so bad. Like I had said something wrong, and I still don't understand what I should have done better. That was almost 30 years ago.

So Feynman's observation that you have to be in some framework that you allow something to be true strikes me as incredibly helpful. I think the MPA must not have had that kind of framework and found herself distressed when she kept reaching for things and never getting something more to hold on to. Maybe I should have had the insight to offer her more of a lifeline.

We might have to watch the whole uncut recording to understand. Perhaps Feynman thought he was talking to the interviewer rather than to you and I and the whole public.

But I have learned something very useful from this non-explanation explanation. Sometimes you have to assume stuff, and sometimes you have to dumb it down. For example, when your five year-old asks you how magnets work, you're just not going to break out Maxwell's equations. Instead you'll explain how everything is made of very tiny things called atoms, and that all atoms are like tiny magnets, but some kinds of atoms can be made to line up and then all the tiny magnet forces add up to a big magnet force. The kid'll eat it up. I know because that's roughly what my father said to me way back when. And so you'll have different explanations for different people, up to the level of your understanding.

The problem here is that not only are we missing context in that clip (had the interviewer been annoying?), but Feynman barely disguises that he can be unpleasant. He has to prep himself to tell the guy that he's just not a physicist. He has to chastise himself for being so good at this that people expect him to be able to explain anything and everything even though it's not always possible. He's kind of an ass here. But what a great answer he gives! His visible annoyance is almost necessary.

I hadn't seen that clip in a long time. Maybe the younger version of me was impressed by it. I understand the spirit of what he's saying. But that clip makes him seem extremely unpleasant. Presenting bits and pieces of the framework is how everybody learns. If somebody slips on ice, I'm not necessarily concerned with why ice is slippery, even though it's a logical part of the reason.

There's plenty of intelligent people who can answer a question like that without devolving into a lecture.

The exact Feynman quote is: "When you explain a 'why', you have to be in some framework in which you allow something to be true."

children.author: Aurornis
children.text:
> The times I have seen the "stochastic parrot" argument used seriously, I could count on one hand.

The person who coined the term and published the Stochastic Parrot paper has been trying to build a career on top of the controversy, publishing books and making a lot of noise on Twitter. For a while it was working and parts of Twitter were bought into the stochastic parrot idea, but the person at the center of it has a bad habit of lashing out at everyone and alienated most of them along the way.

The concept feels antiquated now that we can all access extremely powerful AI models for $20/month and see for ourselves, but there was a time when people took this seriously. I think it was a very convenient argument for those who were in denial, and there was a large audience who wanted to consume ideas that validated their denial.

The times I have seen the "stochastic parrot" argument used seriously, I could count on one hand. But the times I've seen people mock it because it's easier to argue against than well-constructed criticisms...

Look, LLMs are models of the training data lossily compressed in a way that allows interpolating between patterns while decompressing.

A pattern can be "it's better to use int32_t than int", what a for loop in c++ looks like, that testing for primality can be done by trying divisors only until the square root of n, etc. Combining those patterns, an LLM can produce a working is_prime function in c++.

Older LLMs were only able to handle simple patterns so the code was more likely to be verbatim training data, newer LLMs work on deeper, more complex patterns so it's harder to detect where those patterns come from.

Similarly, the list of approaches a mathematician uses to approach a problem is also a pattern. One of them will be proof by induction - how to convert such a proof to Lean will is also a pattern. The idea that induction can be done separately for odd and even cases is also a pattern.

LLMs are no longer generating the final output directly - they are simulating human work but at a much larger scale. That's how they are able to generate novel results.

But it's all based on labor scraped and patternized without consent or credit, let alone monetary compensation.

And I still wouldn't call it intelligence because that gives people the idea that it's something which gives complete, correct and unbiased answers. It's still autocomplete under the hood, there's just more and more tooling built around it to keep it on track, to check intermediate results, to do arithmetic, etc. The LLMs in some cases is more like a heuristic for deterministic tools.

  Status truly is your god, whether you would admit so or not.”
https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/status-is-your-god

There's a book, "Impro", about a theatric studio that practiced improvised sketches. One thing they struggled with was a normal conversation. People have them all the time yet somehow artists could not find the right approach.

One day the head of the studio (the book author) had an insight. She asked the actors to drive the conversation so that they always bump the status of themselves or the other party in any direction, but only a little.

This did the magic. Not only the actors understood her perfectly, the conversation started to flow and could go endlessly while staying amusing and captivating for spectators. (Look up the book for examples.)

After they discovered that secret they started seeing the pattern (status games) everywhere up to the point they asked themselves whether there is anything else in human communication.

This was a British studio, the sketches were mostly comedy.
